replacement: “To hell?” Mitya broke in, and let out his short, abrupt laugh. “Andrey, simple soul,” and he grabbed him by the shoulders again, “tell me, what do you think, will Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov go to hell or not?”
“Oh, sir! I’m afraid of driving you, the way you talk is so strange.”

“Some strangers. One is an official, a gentleman, a Pole by the sound of him. He’s the one who sent the horses from here to fetch her. And there’s another with him, a friend of his or a traveling companion, who can tell. They’re in civilian clothes.”
“Flying it went. How could I forget? You must have left three thousand behind.”

Trifon Borissovitch gave Mitya a wary look, but at once did as he was told. He took him into the passage and went by himself into the first big room, next to the one where the guests sat, and carried away the light. Then he led Mitya in on tiptoe and set him in a dark corner, where he could watch the company freely without being seen. But Mitya did not look for long. In fact he could not see them at all. He saw her. His heart pounded, and everything went dark before his eyes.
